title: Medical-cost exposure is translated into credit visibility, partial reporting relief, and contested federal remedy
source_unit: CFPB Consumer Credit Panel and federal regulatory record

denominator.unit: CFPB Consumer Credit Panel medical-collection tradeline universe; report percentage

observations.method: CFPB descriptive analysis of a 1-in-48 longitudinal sample from one nationwide consumer reporting agency; medical tradelines first reported after January 2017.
observations.uncertainty: One bureau does not cover all collections; percentages are tradeline-level, not household prevalence or causal estimates.
observations.subgroup: Medical collection tradelines in the CFPB Consumer Credit Panel.
observations.counterinterpretation: Low paid status may reflect reporting conventions, settlement, bankruptcy, or payment outside the measured status; it does not alone measure inability to pay.

observations.period: Quarter before and quarter of medical collection reporting; 2017 to 2022

denominator.unit: CFPB Consumer Credit Panel consumers with a newly reported medical collection; report average

observations.method: CFPB compares credit scores in the quarter before and the quarter when a medical collection appears.
observations.uncertainty: Descriptive timing does not isolate the collection from other credit events or establish that the collection caused the full score change.
observations.counterinterpretation: Low pre-reporting scores show selection and prior financial strain; the event-time decline may include other concurrent reporting changes.

observations.period: March 2022; consumers with reported medical collections

denominator.unit: CFPB Consumer Credit Panel consumer universe; report percentage

consumers_likely_to_retain_some_collecti.unit: approximately percent of consumers with medical collections

observations.method: CFPB describes the March 2022 stock of consumers with at least one medical collection and models which consumers would retain a collection under announced low-balance, paid-status, and waiting-period changes.
observations.uncertainty: The residual estimate is modeled under announced reporting changes and is not an observed post-policy household outcome.
observations.subgroup: Consumers in the CFPB Consumer Credit Panel with medical collections.
observations.counterinterpretation: Removal from a credit report changes visibility, not necessarily the underlying balance, care access, or household burden.

observations.period: 2017 to 2022; consumers with medical collections and census-tract distribution

denominator.unit: CFPB Consumer Credit Panel consumer and tract distributions; report percentages

majority_black_tract_share_with_medical_.unit: percent of consumers with medical collections

under_40k_tract_share_with_medical_colle.unit: percent of consumers with medical collections

observations.method: CFPB compares census-tract race and median-income distributions for consumers with medical collections against the full Consumer Credit Panel.
observations.uncertainty: Tract composition is not individual race or income and does not identify why collections or reporting changes are distributed differently.
observations.subgroup: Consumers with medical collections versus all CFPB Consumer Credit Panel consumers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Geographic concentration can reflect coverage, provider markets, income, illness, reporting, and credit composition rather than one mechanism.

observations.period: January to July 2025; federal medical-debt reporting rule

denominator.unit: CFPB Regulation V regulatory action and subsequent court disposition

observations.method: CFPB’s current Regulation V record reports the final rule and the Eastern District of Texas vacatur upon joint request of the Bureau and plaintiffs.
observations.uncertainty: This records legal status, not implementation, state-law variation, future litigation, or household outcome.
observations.counterinterpretation: Vacatur does not establish that prior voluntary reporting changes ended or that every consumer faced the same credit consequence.

boundary: This credit-system and legal-response layer does not link a particular medical bill to a particular care choice, household trade-off, housing/work/insurance outcome, dispute, remedy, trust judgment, political action, or geopolitical consequence.
